analysis.one_liner: Bars credit card companies from raising your rate because of unrelated info on your credit report.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: Senator Tester introduced it in May 2007 and it stayed in the Senate Banking Committee until the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: At the time, credit card companies could raise your interest rate not because you missed a payment on that card, but because of anything negative anywhere in your credit history — a late bill elsewhere, a drop in your credit score, even a new inquiry. This practice was called 'universal default.' The bill would amend the Truth in Lending Act to ban it: a card issuer could only raise your rate or take away a low introductory rate based on what you actually did on that account. It would also require issuers to clearly disclose this limit to cardholders.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card holders, especially those carrying a balance who might otherwise see rates jump from outside events like a dip in their credit score or negative information on their credit report unrelated to the card.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a creditor from using any adverse information about a consumer — including anything in a consumer report or a change in the consumer's credit score — as the basis for increasing a credit card's interest rate, unless the reason is directly related to that account [S2][S3].
Also stops issuers from removing or raising a low introductory rate for reasons unrelated to the account itself [S2][S3].
Requires the credit card issuer to clearly and conspicuously describe this protection to the consumer in required disclosures and statements [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, which lose the ability to raise rates — and collect more interest — based on customers' overall credit profiles rather than their behavior on the card.

drawbacks.text: Restricting rate increases could push issuers to raise rates for everyone or tighten who qualifies for cards at all, since they can no longer price risk based on a customer's broader credit profile [S3].

Cardholders who become riskier on other debts could continue getting the same low rate on this card even as their overall risk rises, a cost that might be spread across other customers through higher rates or fees [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is straightforward: people who pay their card bill on time no longer get penalized for things unrelated to that card, like a dip in their credit score caused by other borrowing. The trade-off is that issuers lose a risk-pricing tool they used to raise revenue, and some of that cost could resurface as higher rates or stricter approval for new customers. For households carrying credit card debt, the protection against surprise rate hikes is the bigger deal.

outcome.mechanism: It died quietly in committee — introduced, read, and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jon Tester introduced the bill on May 3, 2007 [S1][S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day [S5].
No further action was recorded; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1][S5].
The bill drew one cosponsor, an Independent [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers came out ahead: by dying in committee, the bill left them free to keep raising cardholders' rates based on outside credit information. Cardholders who might have been hit with universal-default rate increases are worse off than they would have been under the bill.

for.name: Sen. Jon Tester
for.role: U.S. Senator from Montana; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Banking Committee.

against.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill; it sat in committee with no hearing or markup for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Credit card issuers
against.what_they_did: The bill would have ended their ability to raise cardholders' rates based on outside credit information; the industry opposed legislative bans on universal default during this period.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows no votes and only two sponsors — a Democrat and one Independent cosponsor — so no partisan shape can be measured; the decisive fact is committee inaction, not a floor split.

industries.note: The bill would bar issuers from raising rates or stripping introductory rates based on adverse information unrelated to the account, cutting off a major revenue lever — rate increases triggered by a customer's broader credit profile. That gain comes directly out of cardholders' pockets, so the industry's interest ran against consumers here.

industries.industry: Credit reporting and credit scoring companies
industries.note: Issuers could no longer use consumer report data or credit score changes to justify card rate increases, reducing one use of bureau data. The effect on bureaus is indirect and modest compared with the effect on issuers.
